cards.front: One strand of a DNA molecule reads A T G C C A. Across from it, the partner strand reads {{c1::T A C G G T}}.
cards.back: A pairs with T and C pairs with G, base by base.
cards.why: Each strand fixes its partner, so one strand is enough to rebuild the other.
cards.quote: Because A pairs only with T and C only with G, each strand fixes the base order of its partner.

cards.front: In a cell that is copying its DNA, what does each old strand serve as, and what does that mean?
cards.back: A template: a pattern that sets the base order of a new partner strand.
cards.why: Pairing A with T and C with G makes the partner's order certain.
cards.quote: each old strand is used as a template, a pattern for a new partner

cards.front: After a cell copies one DNA molecule without a mistake, what do the two new molecules look like?
cards.back: Both have the same base order, and each is made of one old strand and one new strand.
cards.why: Each old strand keeps its place and gains a new partner.
cards.quote: the cell gets two copies with the same base order, each made of one old strand and one new one.

cards.front: A piece of DNA is copied once, then both new molecules are copied again. How many molecules result, and how many still contain an original strand?
cards.back: Four molecules, and exactly two contain an original strand.
cards.why: Each round keeps every old strand whole and gives it a new partner.
cards.quote: Each round keeps every old strand whole and gives it a new partner, so the two originals end up in two molecules, however many rounds follow.
cards.section: Explore: unzip and copy a DNA molecule

cards.front: DNA is a polymer, a long chain of repeating units called {{c1::nucleotides}}.
cards.quote: DNA is a polymer, a long chain of repeating units called nucleotides.
cards.section: Explain: a twisted ladder of four bases

cards.front: In a DNA nucleotide, the {{c1::base}} is the part that carries information.
cards.back: The other two parts are the sugar and the phosphate group.
cards.quote: Each is a sugar called deoxyribose, a phosphate group and a base, the part that carries information
cards.section: Explain: a twisted ladder of four bases

cards.front: Name the four bases found in DNA and give their letters.
cards.back: Adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C) and guanine (G).
cards.quote: adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C) or guanine (G).
cards.section: Explain: a twisted ladder of four bases

cards.front: Along one strand of DNA, a {{c1::covalent}} bond joins each sugar to the next phosphate.
cards.back: A covalent bond is a strong bond in which atoms share electrons.
cards.quote: A covalent bond, a strong bond in which atoms share electrons, joins each sugar to the next phosphate along a strand.
cards.section: Explain: a twisted ladder of four bases

cards.front: To copy DNA, the two strands must be pulled apart. Which bonds break, the covalent bonds along each backbone or the hydrogen bonds across the rungs, and why does it matter?
cards.back: The hydrogen bonds across the rungs break. The backbones stay whole, so each old strand keeps its base order and can serve as a template.
cards.why: Hydrogen bonds are weak attractions; covalent bonds are strong.
cards.quote: The weak hydrogen bonds across the rungs break, and the covalent backbones stay whole.
cards.section: Explain: a twisted ladder of four bases

cards.front: Why does a single strand of DNA have a direction?
cards.back: Every nucleotide is bonded to the next the same way round, so the backbone points one way. In a double helix the two strands point opposite ways.
cards.quote: Along a strand, every nucleotide is bonded to the next the same way round, so the backbone has a direction.
cards.section: Explain: a twisted ladder of four bases

cards.front: In what two ways does the zipper analogy for DNA break down?
cards.back: A zipper's teeth carry no message, but the order of DNA's bases does. And a wrong base can occasionally slip into DNA.
cards.quote: The analogy breaks in two places: a zipper's teeth carry no message, while the order of DNA's bases does, and a wrong base can occasionally slip in.
cards.section: Explain: a twisted ladder of four bases

cards.front: What is a gene?
cards.back: A region of DNA whose base order codes for a protein or for an RNA molecule that does a job of its own.
cards.quote: A gene is a region of DNA whose base order codes for a protein or for an RNA molecule that does a job of its own.
cards.section: Explain: a twisted ladder of four bases

cards.front: A {{c1::chromosome}} is one very long DNA molecule wrapped around proteins, and it carries many genes.
cards.quote: A chromosome is one very long DNA molecule wrapped around proteins, and it carries many genes.
cards.section: Explain: a twisted ladder of four bases

cards.front: About what share of human DNA codes for proteins, and what do other stretches do?
cards.back: About 1 to 2 percent. Other stretches control genes or help hold chromosomes in shape; for much of the rest, scientists debate whether it has any job.
cards.quote: Only about 1 to 2 percent of human DNA codes for proteins.
cards.section: Explain: a twisted ladder of four bases

cards.front: Where do plants, animals and fungi keep most of their DNA, and where do bacteria keep theirs?
cards.back: Plants, animals and fungi: mostly in the nucleus. Bacteria: in a nucleoid, a region with no membrane around it.
cards.quote: Bacteria keep their DNA in a nucleoid, a region of the cell with no membrane around it.
cards.section: Explain: a twisted ladder of four bases

cards.front: What does the enzyme that unzips DNA break, and what does it leave intact?
cards.back: It breaks only the hydrogen bonds between the strands. The covalent backbones stay whole.
cards.quote: One enzyme unzips the helix, breaking only the hydrogen bonds.
cards.section: Explain: copying DNA one strand at a time

cards.front: What does DNA polymerase do at each template base?
cards.back: It picks the free nucleotide that pairs with that base and joins it to the new strand with a covalent bond.
cards.why: Picking the pairing partner is why wrong bases almost never get in.
cards.quote: Another enzyme, DNA polymerase, picks the free nucleotide that pairs with each template base, so a wrong one almost never gets in.
cards.section: Explain: copying DNA one strand at a time

cards.front: A real cell opens DNA at a moving Y called a {{c1::fork}}, and the fork's two templates point opposite ways.
cards.quote: It opens a moving Y called a fork, and the fork's two templates point opposite ways.
cards.section: Explain: copying DNA one strand at a time

cards.front: Suppose a cell unzipped its whole DNA molecule before copying it. Would either new strand still have to be built in pieces?
cards.back: No. Both templates would be fully open, so polymerase could copy each in one long run. The pieces come from the moving fork.
cards.quote: With both templates fully open, polymerase could copy each one in one long run.
cards.section: Explain: copying DNA one strand at a time

cards.front: Which three facts together force one new DNA strand to be built in pieces?
cards.back: Polymerase adds nucleotides only at the arrowhead end of a new strand; the two templates point opposite ways; and the fork opens template only a little at a time.
cards.why: Remove any one fact and the pieces are not needed.
cards.quote: The pieces need three facts at once: that rule, templates pointing opposite ways, and a fork that opens template a little at a time.
cards.section: Explain: copying DNA one strand at a time

cards.front: A human cell copies about 6 billion base pairs. At one uncorrected mistake per billion bases copied, about how many uncorrected mistakes appear per copy?
cards.back: Polymerase adds a nucleotide across from every base on both old strands: 2 x 6 billion = 12 billion. At one per billion, that is about 12 mistakes, a rough size rather than an exact count.
cards.quote: A human cell copies roughly 6 billion base pairs, so polymerase adds about 12 billion nucleotides, one across from every base on both old strands.
cards.section: What one in a billion means for one cell

cards.front: Base pairing makes copying possible. What brings the error rate down to about one in a billion bases?
cards.back: The copying enzyme's checks, together with separate repair enzymes.
cards.why: Pairing makes the copy possible; checking makes it accurate.
cards.quote: the copying enzyme's checks and separate repair enzymes bring errors down to about one in a billion bases copied.

cards.front: A wrong A is placed opposite a C on a template and nothing catches it. After the next round of copying, what do the two molecules made from this one look like at that spot?
cards.back: The strand with the C gets a G, keeping the original C-G pair. The strand with the wrong A gets a T, so that molecule now has an A-T pair where C-G was. It looks like a normal pair, so later copies inherit it unless another change happens there.
cards.why: A mismatch is copied as if it were normal once strands are copied separately.
cards.quote: The strand with the C gets a G, keeping the original C-G pair.
cards.section: What one in a billion means for one cell

cards.front: A change in the base order of DNA is called a {{c1::mutation}}, and it can change proteins.
cards.quote: That is a mutation, a change in the base order, and mutations can change proteins.
cards.section: What one in a billion means for one cell

cards.front: In a sample of double-stranded DNA, 30 percent of the bases are A. What percent are G?
cards.back: T is also 30 percent, so A plus T is 60 percent. The other 40 percent is split evenly between G and C, so G is 20 percent.
cards.why: A pairs with T and C pairs with G, so each pair has equal amounts.
cards.quote: a sample of double-stranded DNA should hold as much A as T, and as much G as C.
cards.section: Elaborate: do the bases really pair up?

cards.front: A table gives sea urchin DNA as A 32.8, T 32.1, G 17.7, C 17.3 percent and E. coli DNA as A 24.7, T 23.6, G 26.0, C 25.7 percent. Compare A plus T in each, and say what the data do and do not support.
cards.back: Sea urchin A plus T is 64.9 percent; E. coli is 48.3 percent. In both, A is close to T and G is close to C, which fits base pairing. The mix itself differs by species.
cards.why: Pairing sets what sits opposite what, not how much of each pair a species has.
cards.quote: The rule says nothing about whether A plus T is the same in every species.
cards.section: Elaborate: do the bases really pair up?

cards.front: Plan an investigation to test whether DNA from different tissues of one animal has the same base composition, and whether it differs from another species. Name the independent and dependent variables.
cards.back: Independent: the tissue (chicken liver, chicken muscle) and the species (chicken, wheat). Dependent: the percentage of each base. Hypothesis: if cells copy DNA accurately, the two chicken tissues match and wheat differs. Use repeated measurements and a sample of known composition as a control.
cards.quote: Every cell in an animal's body grows from one fertilized egg by copying DNA.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In a study comparing chicken liver and muscle DNA, the two tissues differ in base composition by far more than repeat measurements of one sample do. What should be suspected first, and why?
cards.back: A problem with the samples or the method. If cells copy DNA accurately, tissues of one animal should match, so a large gap points to the samples or method before anything else.
cards.quote: A large difference between chicken tissues would point to a problem with the samples or the method before anything else.
cards.section: Design problem
